summary: Intro discovery for Sundial Systems evaluating Redwood Private for sensitive inference workloads. Main topics: VPC connectivity patterns, IP space constraints, egress and region gating, key management and audit requirements. Redwood AE + SE walked through tradeoffs between Hosted/Dedicated/Private and proposed pilot plan.
topics: Private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) and IP reservation
Egress / NAT and corporate proxy constraints
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Lyttle (CTO - Sundial), Sofia Chen (Head of Infra), Diego Morales (Net Eng)
Links shared: Redwood private checklist (https://redwood.example.com/private-checklist), security pack (https://redwood.example.com/security-pack), sample network diagram (drive/sundial-network-diagram)

00:00 Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you squeezing this in. Quick intros on our side - I'm Jordan, AE, and Priya is our SE. 
00:12 Priya (SE): Hi all - Priya here, I focus on private deployments and the networking side.
00:18 Mark (CTO): Hey, Mark. Appreciate the time. We've got Sofia and Diego with me.
00:23 Sofia: hi
00:24 Diego: afternoon
00:30 Jordan: Great. High level goal for today: understand Sundial's network constraints and whether Private (VPC) deployment makes sense vs Dedicated. We'll capture next steps and a pilot plan. Sound OK?
00:40 Mark: Yep, sounds good. We're under a bit of time pressure - need a vendor that can meet SOC2 and keep data in our EU region. Latency to users in EU is important.
00:52 Jordan: Understood - we'll cover region gating and also how we handle KMS and audit logs.

04:05 Priya: Could you walk us through the current VPC layout and any CIDR limitations? I know you mentioned narrow IP space in the intake form.
04:14 Sofia: Yeah, we are kind of tight. Our primary infra VPC is a /16 but it's split across many teams; the team owning inference only has a /22 available for workloads. We're trying to allocate small prefixes.
04:30 Priya: Ok that's pretty common. Two approaches: either we do PrivateLink endpoints into Redwood's private dataplane so you only need endpoint ENIs and minimal IPs, or we peer / use transit gateway if you want full routable subnets and egress control. PrivateLink is lighter on IPs but less flexible for cross-subnet routing.
04:55 Diego: For us IPs are gold. We can't spare tons of ENIs per AZ. Also we have strict egress through a corporate proxy - all outbound must hit the proxy in the same VPC or via NAT.
05:10 Jordan: That makes sense. Quick callout: Redwood Private supports both options — PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink) and TGW peering. We typically recommend PrivateLink when CIDR is tight and you want minimal inbound footprint.
05:25 Mark: How does auth work across PrivateLink? Is there a separate VIP or cert exchange?
05:33 Priya: It's a standard interface; traffic flows over interface ENIs and we do mTLS between your side and the service. Authentication is via your API key or token and we can integrate with your identity provider for RBAC. There might be some transcribed noise here, we say m t l s, but it's mutual TLS.

08:00 Sofia: Another constraint — our security team requires keys to be in our KMS or HSM, we can't have Redwood-managed keys for certain workloads. How flexible is the KMS integration?
08:12 Jordan: We support two modes: customer-managed keys via external KMS/HSM (we have integrations with AWS KMS and bring-your-own HSM patterns) and Redwood-managed for lower friction. For the pilot we can use customer KMS if you want to validate encrypt-at-rest and key rotation policies.
08:30 Diego: And audit logs? We need request-level logging and immutable audit trails forwarded to our logging cluster.
08:36 Priya: Yes, Private includes audit logging exports — we can push logs to your S3 buckets or to a logging endpoint via TLS. We'll share the schema.

11:10 Mark: Slightly related — network egress. Our compliance team wants all egress to be deterministic and go through a set of IP ranges we control. If Redwood is hosted in our VPC via PrivateLink, how do we ensure egress doesn't leak to other regions?
11:25 Priya: Good question. With PrivateLink, you control outbound since traffic goes from your subnets to the ENIs. For cases where Redwood needs to call external services on your behalf (e.g., model stores), we can pin region and restrict egress to your peered endpoints. For Dedicated or Hosted, you'd rely on our routing policies and we can provide fixed egress IPs for enterprise tiers.

14:00 Diego: About region gating — we must ensure model inference and token data do not leave EU. Is the Redwood private control plane in our VPC or does it still talk to a Redwood control plane?
14:14 Jordan: For Private we offer a split model: control plane can be in Redwood's managed control plane (but you can opt for a private control plane deployed into your VPC for fully air-gapped setups). The data plane (inference) can be pinned to EU regions. For the pilot, many customers use the managed control plane but restrict data plane to the region. If you need fully private control plane we can discuss on-prem package.
14:40 Sofia: That helps. I want to see the architectural patterns — private control plane vs managed-control-plane with VPC-only data plane.

17:20 Priya: I'll sketch three patterns: 1) PrivateLink into Redwood multi-tenant dataplane (minimal IP), 2) TGW attachment to dedicated customer project (more IPs but full routing), 3) Fully private control plane in your account (full isolation). Each has tradeoffs on latency, ops burden, and cost.
17:45 Mark: Latency is a big factor for us. If we use PrivateLink into a Redwood EU cluster, what's typical p99 latency delta?
18:00 Priya: Depends on model and batch size, but for chat-style models we've seen p95 token latencies in the low single-digit tens of ms within-region. PrivateLink overhead is minimal — network hop and ENI NAT is usually <5ms additional. The bigger delta is if you go cross-region.
18:20 Diego: If we do TGW and route directly, do we have to expose a subnet on our side for Redwood to place instances?
18:29 Priya: With TGW, Redwood would deploy in a customer-dedicated VPC (or provide a routed VPC) and you'd peer via TGW. That means more routable IPs and you can egress through your NATs. IP planning is the heavy lift there.

21:00 Jordan: Quick commercial note — Dedicated gives reserved capacity with predictable throughput, Private gives isolation and VPC integration. For pilot we typically do a short Dedicated pilot or Private pilot depending on networking. Pricing sheet coming in the follow-up.

23:40 Sofia: We also have an internal requirement to avoid NAT gateway costs spiking. If PrivateLink is used, does that create lots of egress to the internet from Redwood's side or from ours?
23:55 Priya: With PrivateLink, traffic stays within AWS network between your VPC and our service endpoints. Your egress to the internet shouldn't increase; any downstream calls Redwood makes out to third parties would be from our side unless you configure service chaining. We'll clarify in the doc.

26:10 Diego: One operational ask: we need a predictable number of ENIs per AZ so we can request IPs. How many ENIs per endpoint and per AZ does Redwood require?
26:22 Priya: Typically it's 1 ENI per PrivateLink endpoint per AZ and a small number of scaling ENIs behind it. For a cluster sized for inference, plan for a handful per AZ. We'll provide a concrete table: endpoints vs expected ENIs and IP counts.

29:40 Mark: On the security front, SSO and RBAC. We use SAML. Can Redwood hook into our IdP?
29:50 Jordan: Yes, we integrate SAML/SSO for the Console and role bindings; for data-plane tokens you can layer on your own token exchange. We'll include the SSO setup guide.

32:00 Diego: Edge case — we run some on-prem workers in a colo that only peer via VPN to our VPC. Could we connect those and still have inference in a private dataplane?
32:10 Priya: As long as your on-prem can route to the VPC where the PrivateLink ENIs live (or the TGW attachments), yes. Latency will factor. For heavy throughput we'd recommend colocating the inference in the region nearest users.

34:30 Jordan: I want to call out two red flags from our side: 1) if you cannot provide any routable IPs for endpoints or subnets, PrivateLink is the only option but it may limit debugging; 2) if you require total air-gap with no managed control plane, that pushes toward our private control plane offering which has longer lead time.

36:55 Sofia: Noted. For compliance, we need proof of SOC2 and ISO and an architecture review. Where do we get those docs?
37:03 Jordan: We'll attach the security pack; it includes SOC2 attestations, ISO references, and our SOC auditor contact. Link is in the meeting notes.

39:40 Diego: One more technical question — we do KV cache warmups and would like to pin certain model caches to local disks. Does Redwood expose local disk mounts or is KV strictly in-memory/external?
39:55 Priya: Currently the runtime exposes a KV cache that sits in memory and optionally on NVMe ephemeral storage within the instance. For Private we can coordinate the instance type and local disk profiles; we do not recommend relying on long-lived disks unless you're on Dedicated with attached persistent options. (transcription: 'k v cash' sometimes mis-heard)

42:15 Mark: Ok, looks like the path is PrivateLink pilot unless we can free up more IPs quickly. Diego will run IP export and Sofia will assign the security reviewer.
42:30 Sofia: yes I'll loop in the security reviewer and infra lead.
42:35 Diego: I'll pull CIDRs and NAT details and send to Jordan.

45:00 Jordan: For the pilot we propose: 1) PrivateLink in EU region with a small inference cluster, 2) customer KMS integration, 3) audit log forwarding to your S3, 4) a 2-hour bench to capture p95/p99 and token costs.
45:18 Mark: Sounds good. Can you also enumerate fallback options if latency or cost is unacceptable?
45:26 Priya: Yep — fallback A is TGW with dedicated routable subnets; fallback B is Dedicated reserved nodes in a customer-dedicated project. We'll include a decision matrix.

48:40 Jordan: Recap of next steps: I'll send the pricing and checklist, Priya will send the sample IP plan and endpoint ENI table, Diego will share CIDRs, Sofia will share reviewer contact. Schedule bench for week of May 11.
48:55 Mark: Thanks, that timeline works.
49:05 Sofia: thanks everyone
49:10 Diego: thanks
49:15 Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email and attach the docs.

Transcript notes: occasional mis-attributions and transcription errors present (e.g., 'k v cash' for KV cache, 'm t l s' tokenization).
